articles.title: ‘Any one who sleeps over his right is bound to suffer’: Chhattisgarh high court rejects 30-year-old salary arrears claim
articles.summary: RAIPUR: The Chhattisgarh high court has dismissed a writ petition seeking payment of alleged salary arrears dating back to 1989-94, holding that a
articles.body: RAIPUR: The Chhattisgarh high court has dismissed a writ petition seeking payment of alleged salary arrears dating back to 1989-94, holding that a litigant must approach the court within a reasonable time, even though no limitation period is prescribed for filing a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution.Justice Bibhu Datta Guru dismissed the petition in limine on October 6 on the grounds of delay and laches, noting that the petitioner had failed to explain why he waited more than three decades to pursue the alleged dues of his late father.The court observed that “a person invoking the extraordinary and discretionary jurisdiction of this Court under Article 226 of the Constitution of India must approach the Court with due diligence and within a reasonable period of time”. It added that writ jurisdiction was not intended to revive stale claims after prolonged inaction.The petitioner, claiming to be the son of a deceased South Eastern Coalfields Ltd (SECL) employee, had sought a direction to the authorities to consider an alleged representation submitted by his father in 1996 for payment of arrears for the period from 1989 to 1994.The court noted that the employee retired in 2002 and died in 2015. Neither he during his lifetime nor the petitioner later took effective steps to pursue the alleged pending representation.Justice Guru said the principles underlying the doctrine of delay and laches were based on “repose, certainty and finality”. Overlooking an enormous delay, the court observed, could prejudice the rights and interests of other parties and unsettle matters that had otherwise attained finality.The petitioner claimed that his father had submitted a representation dated January 2, 1996. However, the court noted that “there is neither any acknowledgement nor any receipt on the record” to establish that it had been submitted to the competent authority.It also found no satisfactory explanation for the delay and said no exceptional circumstances had been presented to justify overlooking it.In a strong observation, the court said: “The petitioner (son of the deceased employee) chose to sleep and got up at his own leisure, for some reason which is fathomable to him only. But such fathoming of reasons by oneself is not countenanced in law.”It added: “Any one who sleeps over his right is bound to suffer.”The court also noted inconsistencies in the petitioner's pleadings. While he claimed that his father had been appointed as an assistant teacher, the alleged representation described him as a peon, Category-II.Holding that the claim concerned alleged arrears more than three decades old and that the petitioner had failed to establish submission of the 1996 representation or provide a plausible explanation for the prolonged inaction, the court declined to exercise its extraordinary writ jurisdiction.“Though there is no period of limitation provided for filing a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution of India, yet ordinarily a writ petition should be filed within a reasonable time,” the court said before dismissing the petition in limine on the ground of delay and laches.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Raipur | Silver Rate in Raipur | Bank Holidays in Raipur | Public Holidays in Raipur | Raipur AQI | Weather in Raipur | Petrol Price in Raipur | Diesel Price in Raipur | CNG Price in Raipur | LPG Price in RaipurStay updated with the latest Raipur news. articles.title: Decision to shift Prajwal to Hindalga prison withheld
articles.summary: Karnataka prison officials withheld plans to shift jailed ex-Hassan MP Prajwal Revanna to Hindalga, citing no DIG to supervise; eight others to move.
articles.body: Bengaluru: Prison authorities’ decision to shift imprisoned former Hassan MP Prajwal Revanna to Hindalga prison in Belagavi was withheld at the last moment Friday.Prior to this, a decision to shift nine convicts from Bengaluru central prison, including Prajwal Revanna, to different jails had been announced. The decision had been made based on a request made by Bengaluru police who had, during raids, recovered mobile phones, sim cards and other electronic items from the convicts, including Prajwal.Director general of police (prisons and correctional services) Alok Kumar told TOI that the decision to shift Prajwal to Hindalga was cancelled at the last moment. “Yes, we had decided to shift Prajwal and eight others to different prisons on the request made by the city police. Prajwal’s shifting to Hindalga was cancelled at the last moment as there is no deputy inspector general (DIG) of prisons. Convicts like Prajwal facing such allegations should be monitored closely under the supervision of a DIG. Therefore, we cancelled it. articles.title: Early release scheme prisoner jailed days after leaving
articles.summary: Michael Bogle had said outside prison last week that "people like me" should not be jailed "for a long time".
articles.body:
A man has been jailed for a number of shoplifting offences days after being freed under the government's early release scheme.

Michael Bogle, 38, was released from HMP Wandsworth on 1 October as part of the first wave of prisoners to be let out under the plan.

Speaking to reporters outside the prison following his release, Bogle said the conditions inside were "awful" and said "people like me" should not be in prison "for a long time".

In the four days after his release, Bogle stole more than £100 worth of detergent from supermarkets in north London.

He was arrested on Tuesday and admitted the offences in court on Wednesday, resulting in an eight-month sentence.

The previous 32-week sentence he was released from early had been suspended but he was jailed for breaching its terms. He served 78 days.

Asked if he had a message for Prime Minister Andy Burnham after his early release, Bogle said: "Keep the early release going. It's good."

The scheme was brought in to relieve pressure on prisons across England and Wales which were dangerously close to reaching full capacity.

It is understood the force's highest ranking commander in north-west London referred to his case in a letter raising concerns about the early releases.

Det Ch Supt Luke Williams outlined the details of the "astonishing" case in correspondence to local politicians, which was later shared by Shadow Home Secretary Chris Philp.

Without naming Bogle, the letter, sent on Wednesday, said he had been identified as a high-risk offender by the probation service but was released on 1 October.

"Just one day after his release" he was recorded on CCTV stealing, Williams said.

'Overcrowded' and 'set up to fail': Freed prisoners react to early release scheme

Is there a way of stopping repeat shoplifting?

How the new prison release scheme will work - and number of inmates to be freed

Following reports from supermarket staff that the offending continued over the following days, neighbourhood officers "spent an entire day" locating the man and bringing him into custody, the letter said.

Williams said: "While I am sure it is not surprising that someone with this history went onto reoffend, the speed with which he did so, and the impact on front-line policing, is astonishing."

"The concerning nature of the Early Release Scheme in this case was a known prolific offender being put back into the community, only to immediately reoffend," Williams said.

"Not only does this place communities at risk but puts demand straight back into policing who must arrest, investigate and put the individual into custody."

He said this case required 27 officer hours to investigate at a cost of £1,887.

Williams told the MPs and councillors that the Met "fully recognises that the government is dealing with significant pressures" in the prison system but that those pressures are being "transferred on to policing with no recognition".

He said the case was "not just a localised issue", but one being seen by Met officers across the capital.

A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said: "We inherited a prison system on the brink of collapse. If we had failed to act, the police would have been forced to halt arrests, putting communities at untold risk.

"We will never jeopardise public safety. That is why we are putting thousands more Neighbourhood Police officers on to our streets, upping police funding to £18.5bn and taking investment in the probation service to record levels."

They added that offenders released early on licence faced the "toughest-ever controls", including exclusion zones and the expansion of electronic tagging.

articles.title: With nothing to lose, Republicans still put America last
articles.summary: A recent Senate resolution requiring the State Department to report on Israeli violence in the West Bank failed to pass despite broad Democratic support and the death of several U.S. citizens since 2022.
articles.body:
Last week, the Senate voted on a resolution would force the State Department to produce a report on Israeli violence in the West Bank. The legislation would require the State Department to report on human rights in countries receiving American security funds within 30 days. If the department fails to produce a report in time, those funds halt automatically.

West Bank violence is of particular interest to some lawmakers for good reason. For one, that violence has reached an “all-time high” which “ threatens mass atrocities.” Second, the United States has the power to stop it. While West Bank attacks are typically committed by Israeli settlers, Israel’s government enables these crimes. It avoids confronting settlers as a matter of policy and even arms their attacks. That’s why Israeli human rights watchdog B’Tselem characterizes settler attacks as “state violence.” As its largest benefactor, the United States could pressure that state to shape up.

This is all the more pressing because Americans are increasingly the victims. Since 2022, at least nine U.S. citizens have been killed in the West Bank. None of the perpetrators have faced accountability. It’s a striking trend: a foreign government, funded and armed by the United States, killing Americans without repercussion. You’d think lawmakers would unanimously be desperate for answers. But you would be wrong.

The resolution failed on a 47-51 vote. Democrats, with the sole and unsurprising exception of Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania, universally supported the resolution. All it would’ve taken was a few Republican votes to pass. The measure only got one: Sen. Rand Paul of Kentucky. With the resolution’s fate resting in Republican hands, the conference closed ranks almost to a man.

It was a gut check for the GOP. The party of “America First” had a golden opportunity to affirm its patriotism. The resolution was their chance to show the world American lives take precedence over laundering a foreign country’s image. And it was a layup. The resolution simply required a report that, coming from the Trump State Department, probably would’ve been a whitewash anyway. It wouldn’t be some revelation that shattered Israel’s popularity or irreparably damaged the American-Israeli alliance. This was a freebie — a morally obvious and politically costless stand.

Domestically, it’s hard to imagine how anyone could object to seeking answers regarding American deaths abroad. Explaining to your constituents why you voted yes wouldn’t be hard. If anything, it’d be hard to explain voting no, which calls your loyalty to this country into question.

Yet Republicans voted no anyway. This wasn’t out of character; the GOP regularly undermines its own “America First” branding. It was nonetheless notable, though, for its nakedness. With other violations of “America First,” there is at least some deniability — however implausible. Take the ongoing war on Iran. Opponents have cast the administration’s ready willingness to bear the entanglement’s immense domestic costs as putting America last. But the administration and its supporters argue that this war is necessary for American security, which Iran threatens existentially. That’s wrong; but it’s a story. A shred of contestability can go a long way.

Similar mental gymnastics were at play when President Trump waived his aid pause for a $20-billion bailout of Argentina. The optics were undeniably poor: sending huge sums to keep afloat a fiscally reckless foreign government as Americans languish. But the administration had an answer. This too was “America First” — a strategic loan (not handout) to counter Chinese influence, maintaining American primacy in its “backyard.” Or, at least, that’s what they claimed . Feel free to dispute it. But there was some narrative that reconciled the move with the GOP’s nationalist marketing.

With the resolution on Israel, there simply isn’t one. Republicans are just nakedly taking the side of a foreign power. No “America First” story is even the least bit plausible here. It’s exactly what it seems.

Last week’s vote largely flew under the radar. But it was highly consequential for the conservative movement. It proved, beyond a shadow of a doubt, that their rallying cry is hollow. “America First” doesn’t denote any genuine commitment to prioritizing this land or its people. If it was even the least bit literal, the resolution would’ve passed resoundingly. But it didn’t. The pledge is remarkably devoid of content. Even when America First-ers have nothing to lose, they won’t abide by it. You often hear people critique the empty sloganeering of the left. But there is no slogan in United States politics more empty than “America First.”

Elias Khoury is a University of Michigan law graduate and freelance writer based in Arlington, Virginia. He also holds a graduate degree in public policy from the London School of Economics.

articles.title: Idaho family has farmed 1,000 acres since 1950; after the state largely shut off its irrigation water in 2025, the owners say crops failed and are now suing to protect the family farm
articles.summary: An Idaho family that has farmed 1,000 acres near the Snake River for three generations has sued the state after an emergency water order forced them to
articles.body: An Idaho family that has farmed 1,000 acres near the Snake River for three generations has sued the state after an emergency water order forced them to shut off their irrigation pumps. The order dried their fields and destroyed their crops. Jerry Bingham and his family have grown wheat, alfalfa, and potatoes near Blackfoot since 1950. They filed a lawsuit in the Seventh Judicial District Court of Idaho in Bingham County. The lawsuit challenges an order from the Idaho Department of Water Resources (IDWR) that stopped groundwater pumping across large areas of the Eastern Snake River Plain. The Binghams are represented by the nonprofit public interest law group Pacific Legal Foundation. They argue that state regulators broke Idaho's long-standing water priority laws and effectively took their private property rights without paying them.Emergency order cuts off groundwaterThe dispute began with an administrative order from IDWR Director Matthew Weaver. Under the order, groundwater users in the Eastern Snake River Basin with water rights dated after 1900 had to stop pumping unless they were part of an approved mitigation district or had their own mitigation plan. The state agency issued the shutdown because water levels in the underground aquifer were falling. It also wanted to meet demands for water from senior surface-water users, including canal companies farther downstream. The Binghams have a 1950 water right. That makes their right older than those of many water users in the region, but newer than surface-water claims from the 19th century. Idaho follows a "first in time, first in right" system for water. Under this system, when there is not enough water, regulators are supposed to limit junior water rights in reverse order of priority. They are not supposed to issue broad bans based simply on historical dates. According to court documents filed by the Pacific Legal Foundation, the state's blanket 1900 cutoff ignored water rights with dates between older and newer claims. The foundation said this unfairly grouped 1950 water-right holders like the Binghams with people who received their water rights much more recently.Crops fail as soil dries outThe effect on the Bingham family farm was immediate and serious. After the state ordered the irrigation pumps to be turned off, the soil across their 1,000 acres dried during the height of the growing season. Important food crops, including wheat and alfalfa, dried up in the heat. The family said they could no longer plant crops, putting their farming business, which has lasted for generations, at risk of permanent failure. Since the first shutdown order, state regulators have allowed the Binghams to turn on their irrigation pumps only once, during a short period in April 2026. The family submitted five different mitigation plans to IDWR. They hoped to legally resume irrigation while still meeting the state's water conservation goals. Regulators rejected all five proposals. With the restrictions continuing and their fields empty, the family decided to sue the state.Constitutional challenge over property rightsIn their petition for judicial review and request to pause enforcement, the Binghams argue that Idaho water rights are real property protected by both the state and federal constitutions. The lawsuit says IDWR unlawfully took their property by denying them access to their established 1950 water allocation without following the state's required curtailment procedures or paying them for their financial losses. Pacific Legal Foundation Senior Attorney Damien Schiff said the case involves more than whether one farm can survive. He said it raises larger questions about government power and the future of farming. "The case is about more than one family's farm. It asks whether the institutions governing scarce resources will give people the certainty to invest, steward those resources responsibly, and produce an abundant future, or whether arbitrary decisions will make all three harder," Schiff said in a public statement released by the foundation.Broader struggle over Snake River BasinThe lawsuit in Bingham County is part of a growing conflict between groundwater users and surface-water users across Southern Idaho. The Eastern Snake Plain Aquifer covers nearly 10,000 square miles. It supplies both deep farm wells and the Snake River. Years of drought, changing rainfall patterns, and more efficient irrigation methods have reduced the amount of water flowing back into the underground aquifer. As a result, downstream canal operators with 19th-century water rights have called for state regulators to step in. In September 2025, a state district judge approved a settlement in a related water dispute. The agreement required some junior groundwater users to stop irrigation for the rest of that season, according to an official news release from the Idaho Department of Water Resources. However, individual family farms that did not join large groundwater districts were left without administrative options when state shutdown orders took effect. The Binghams are asking the court to stop enforcement of the state's pumping ban on their property and restore a clear, legal system for deciding water rights across Idaho. The case remains pending in the Seventh Judicial District Court.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Four jailed after man kidnapped in Birmingham and set on fire
articles.summary: Tomasz Samel was kidnapped and attacked over the loss of illicit cigarettes worth £1m.
articles.body:
Warning: This article contains details that readers may find distressing

Four men have been jailed for killing a member of an organised crime group who was tortured, doused in petrol and set alight.

Father-of-two Tomasz Samel, 45, was kidnapped in March 2019 in Birmingham by three men claiming to be from Interpol, before being driven to the Liverpool area and attacked over the loss of illicit cigarettes worth £1m.

Passing sentence at Birmingham Crown Court, Judge Mr Justice Wall said Samel "was vulnerable at the time he was set alight – he was naked and outnumbered".

Neil Jones, 49, of no fixed address, and Tobiasz Kozlowski, 38, from Kirkby, Merseyside, were jailed for life after being convicted in August of murder and conspiracy to cause grievous bodily harm .

The pair pleaded guilty to conspiracy to kidnap and conspiracy to falsely imprison before the trial began, while Jones had also admitted manslaughter.

Kevin Wooden, 46, of Banbury, Oxfordshire, and Kye Arthur, 35, from Lockleaze, Bristol, who were found guilty of manslaughter after being cleared of murder and conspiracy to cause grievous bodily harm, were given 23 years and 22 years respectively.

They had previously admitted conspiracy to kidnap and conspiracy to falsely imprison.

Kozlowski's wife, Sandra Kozlowska, 38, also from Kirkby, was convicted of assisting an offender by helping him to avoid detection by police, hiding evidence and moving money.

She received a three-year prison sentence, suspended for three years.

Samel's killing was linked to the seizure of illicit and counterfeit cigarettes which had been smuggled into the UK from Poland.

HM Revenue and Customs seized the cigarettes from a unit he kept in Elkington Street, in the Aston area of Birmingham, during a raid in February 2019.

During the sentencing Wall told the defendants they had all chosen to involve themselves in a "truly horrific series of events".

He described Kozlowski and Jones as the "organisers" and said they had a "motive to punish" Samel due to the financial stake they had in the missing cigarettes.

Samel, who was the subject of an international arrest warrant, was kidnapped from his home in Raleigh Road, Handsworth, on 27 March 2019.

"I am sure that the two of you intended that Mr Samel would die," Wall added, telling the court he had been "stripped naked, and, while seated and defenceless, petrol was thrown over him and he was set alight".

"He suffered extensive burns to most of his body," the judge added.

After being set on fire he was dumped in a remote area of Lancashire, where he managed to walk to a house in the village of Bickerstaffe to ask for help. He was taken to Whiston Hospital in Prescot but died on 21 June 2019.

Wooden and Arthur were paid to kidnap the man, along with a third person who has not yet been identified, Wall said, adding that it was impossible to say how Samel was treated before being set alight due to his burn injuries.

He also stated Samel was in hospital for almost three months before he died and said: "The level of his suffering between the time at which the injuries were inflicted and his death is difficult to imagine."

A police investigation saw inquiries carried out in Poland, Greece, the Dominican Republic, Mexico, Colombia, France, Scotland and Wales, where the gang had operations or had fled to in the aftermath of the kidnap.

The CPS said Wooden was arrested in the Dominican Republic under a false name and had to be extradited before the trial.

articles.title: A Texas ranch spanning nearly 77,000 acres is back on the market for $180 million after the 2024 Smokehouse Creek Fire scorched more than half its land; the property has since undergone a major recovery
articles.summary: According to reporting from the Fort Worth Business Journal, CoStar News and DTN, the historic Turkey Track Ranch in the Texas Panhandle has returned to
articles.body: According to reporting from the Fort Worth Business Journal, CoStar News and DTN, the historic Turkey Track Ranch in the Texas Panhandle has returned to the market for $180 million after being pulled from sale following the devastating 2024 Smokehouse Creek Fire. The 77,721-acre property has since undergone extensive restoration, including the rebuilding of roughly 65 miles of fencing and the return of its cattle operation. The ranch, which stretches from the Caprock to the Canadian River, is being marketed by Dallas-based Icon Global. The current offering includes a 25% mineral stake and places the property among the largest ranches currently available for sale in Texas.A ranch shaped by water, cattle and historyTurkey Track is far more than a vast stretch of open range. About 26 miles of the Canadian River run through the property, while eight major creek basins, natural springs and 64 water wells provide resources for livestock and wildlife. Five irrigation pivots cover about 838 acres, and the ranch sits above the Ogallala Aquifer, one of the most important groundwater systems in the Great Plains.The property also contains cropland, grazing land and infrastructure supporting a large cattle operation. Its combination of agricultural production, water resources, wildlife habitat and mineral interests is a major part of the ranch’s appeal to prospective buyers.Its history stretches back to the late 19th century. The Turkey Track brand dates to 1878, while W.T. Coble acquired the original headquarters in 1916. The property has remained associated with the Coble and Whittenburg families for more than a century.The ranch also encompasses land connected to the 1864 and 1874 battles of Adobe Walls, important episodes in the history of the Texas Panhandle and the wider conflict between Indigenous peoples, settlers and the U.S. military.The wildfire changed the saleTurkey Track was already being marketed before disaster struck. The property had first gone on the market in 2021 for $200 million and was later offered at $180 million. Sale negotiations were underway in 2024 when the Smokehouse Creek Fire swept across the region.The fire began on February 26, 2024, after a utility pole failed and power lines fell near the ranch’s boundary, according to findings cited by Texas officials and Xcel Energy filings. The resulting fire complex ultimately burned roughly 1.05 million acres across the Texas Panhandle and into Oklahoma, making it the largest wildfire recorded in Texas.Around 46,000 acres of Turkey Track’s rangeland were affected, representing roughly 60% of the property. The ranch was subsequently taken off the market while the owners focused on recovery. The wider disaster killed three people, destroyed hundreds of structures and resulted in the deaths of thousands of cattle. Texas later sued Southwestern Public Service, an Xcel Energy subsidiary, alleging that poorly maintained infrastructure caused the fire.Back on the marketNearly three years after the fire, the ranch’s owners have decided the property is ready for another attempt at a sale. Native vegetation and pastures have returned, wildlife has rebounded and cattle operations have resumed. The restoration also included approximately 65 miles of new fencing across the sprawling property.The asking price is once again $180 million, putting the ranch’s current value at roughly $2,300 per acre. For a buyer, the offering combines scale, agricultural production, water, mineral interests and a history that is unusually concentrated in a single property. Turkey Track is now being presented not simply as land that survived one of Texas’ most destructive wildfires, but as a working ranch that has emerged from the disaster ready for its next chapter.A Texas ranch spanning nearly 77,000 acres is back on the market for $180 million after the 2024 Smokehouse Creek Fire scorched more than half its land; the property has since undergone a major recoveryReady to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: International Criminal Court ‘firmly rejects’ new US sanctions
articles.summary: The International Criminal Court (ICC) strongly pushed back on Friday after the U.S. imposed new sanctions on its financial assets, slamming the move as “an assault on the rule of law.” ICC President Tomoko Akane said in a video shared to the court’s website that it “firmly rejects” the U.S.’s retaliation, which Secretary of State…
articles.body:
The International Criminal Court (ICC) strongly pushed back on Friday after the U.S. imposed new sanctions on its financial assets, slamming the move as “an assault on the rule of law.”

ICC President Tomoko Akane said in a video shared to the court’s website that it “firmly rejects” the U.S.’s retaliation, which Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced Friday morning as former ICC judge Navi Pillay was awarded a Nobel Peace Prize. The Trump administration previously sanctioned Akane in August.

Akane called the latest financial penalties an “attack” on the countries that created the ICC and on international legal order.

“It is an attack on the victims of mass atrocities who have waited years, sometimes decades, for those to be held to account,” she said.

The international judicial body, based in The Hague, Netherlands, was created in 2002 to address global atrocities when countries are unable or fail to intervene.

The ICC has pursued war crimes cases against U.S.-allied Israel over its military offensive in Gaza. Pillay, who received Nobel recognition for her contributions to boosting the impact of international law, recently oversaw a United Nations report that concluded that Israeli forces committed genocide in the region.

In a video shared on social media announcing these sanctions, Rubio cited the court’s efforts to prosecute American citizens, despite the U.S. not being a member of the ICC.

“We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling their ability to operate against us,” Rubio said. “Because our message is clear: the United States and the American people are not subject to the jurisdiction of this fake ICC.”

Rubio also called on U.S. allies who are members of the ICC to “rein in this rogue court.”

Akane said that global leadership must now choose between “a world where might is right” or “a future based on the rule of law.”

“In the face of such attacks, we cannot remain indifferent. All of us, including state parties, have a legal and moral duty to act in defense of the international order,” the judge said. “To stand up for law, not force. We will be judged by history for the choices we make today.”

“I pledge to you: The International Criminal Court will continue its work undeterred, with the firm resolve that justice must prevail,” she continued.

United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk also denounced the Trump administration’s sanctions on the ICC as “unacceptable” and called for the U.S. to withdraw them in a statement his office released Friday.

“It is abundantly clear in all the conflicts and crises that plague our world that impunity fuels violence and suffering,” Türk said. “We need to be investing more in ensuring justice and accountability — rather than penalizing those who are documenting, investigating and prosecuting serious violations.”

articles.title: A New York house built in 1728 was hidden inside later storefronts and saved from demolition in 2013; after a 13-year, $3 million restoration, Albany's oldest building has reopened to the public
articles.summary: For decades, one of Albany’s oldest homes was hiding in plain sight.
articles.body: For decades, one of Albany’s oldest homes was hiding in plain sight. The Van Ostrande-Radliff House, built in 1728, had been absorbed into later commercial buildings and concealed behind storefronts as the neighbourhood changed around it. Its historic importance became clearer only after neighbouring structures were demolished and the house’s distinctive Dutch architecture was revealed. Now, after more than 13 years of planning, fundraising and construction, the building has reopened as a public space. The restoration cost more than $3 million and has given the 48 Hudson Avenue property a new purpose as the headquarters of the Historic Albany Foundation. The Times Union and the foundation’s official reopening announcement describe the project as a remarkable effort to preserve Albany’s Dutch architectural roots. Read more details about it here, as per the reports:A house hidden by the city’s growthThe Van Ostrande-Radliff House was built by Johannes Van Ostrande, an alderman who constructed the small home on the southern edge of Albany, only a few hundred yards from the original Fort Orange. At the time, the building stood in a much less developed part of the city. Its timber frame featured large H-shaped structures known as H-bents, while two jambless fireplaces helped heat the compact interior.By modern standards, the original home was remarkably small. It measured approximately 23 by 33 feet and included one large room on the ground floor, along with two upper lofts that were used for attic storage. The lower level was made of brick, while the upper section and steep roof were covered in pine shakes. Its simple design reflected the building methods and needs of Albany’s early Dutch settlers.A few years after the house was built, Johannes Radliff, a cobbler, purchased the property. He widened the structure to make room for a carriage passage and raised the roof to create a full second floor. The house continued to evolve as Albany expanded, eventually becoming part of a much larger commercial property, as per the reports.From family home to business addressDuring the 19th century, Jared Holt added a three-story brick extension to the property for his leather goods business. Another addition was later attached to the rear by dry goods merchant George T. Stoneman. These changes gradually covered the original structure and made it appear more like a typical commercial building from a later era.By the 20th century, 48 Hudson Avenue had become home to several businesses. The decision became particularly important three years later, when the neighbouring building at 50 Hudson Avenue was demolished after being considered at risk of collapse.The survival of the Van Ostrande-Radliff House was not guaranteed. The building had endured floods, fires, commercial alterations and changing development pressures. Its preservation required the foundation and its supporters to look beyond the cost and difficulty of the work and recognise the value of retaining a physical link to Albany’s earliest communities.The restoration took more than 13 years and was supported by grants from the New York State Office of Parks, Recreation and Historic Preservation and Empire State Development. Additional grants, private donations and state historic tax credits also helped fund the project, according to the Times Union.A careful restorationThe restoration involved far more than cosmetic repairs. Workers stabilised the house with new foundation walls, restored its historic timber framing and lowered the Dutch roof to bring it closer to its original proportions. The front wall was rebuilt using custom Dutch-dimension bricks, helping the exterior reflect the construction techniques associated with the building’s early history.The goal was to preserve the structure rather than create a modern imitation. Visitors can still see the physical evidence of the house’s age, including its timber framework and the way later additions were built around the original home. The result allows people to experience an authentic survivor of Albany’s colonial past.Schuyler Bull, a Historic Albany Foundation board member, told the Times Union that visitors were not entering a modern recreation of history. Instead, they were seeing a piece of Albany that had survived intact. The Historic Albany Foundation announced that the original portion of the building would serve as classroom and event space, while also housing the foundation’s research library.The later additions now accommodate the foundation’s Architectural Parts Warehouse, a satellite Tool Lending Library and administrative offices. This adaptive reuse means the building will remain active rather than becoming a preserved shell that visitors can see only occasionally.The official Historic Albany Foundation announcement invited the public to tour the building and meet the people involved in its restoration. The house will remain open for tours and drop-in visits, offering visitors an opportunity to see how Dutch settlers built in Albany nearly 300 years ago.Preserving more than bricksThe reopening has given Albany a building that tells several stories at once. It reflects the city’s Dutch beginnings, the growth of commercial neighbourhoods and the many families and businesses that occupied the property over the centuries. Its layered appearance also shows how historic buildings can change without losing every trace of their original identity.For the Historic Albany Foundation, the project demonstrates why preservation remains important in a rapidly changing city. By saving the Van Ostrande-Radliff House, the organisation has preserved not only an architectural landmark but also evidence of the people, skills and communities that shaped Albany.Nearly three centuries after Johannes Van Ostrande built the small timber-framed home, the property has entered another chapter. articles.body:
The Flydubai co-pilot who attacked the plane’s captain with an axe last month intended to crash the aircraft into a passenger terminal at an Israeli airport, according to authorities in the United Arab Emirates.

The suspect, identified as 29-year-old Omani national Hamam al-Hammami, planned to seize control of the 182-passenger aircraft and crash it into the terminal at Ben Gurion Airport near Tel Aviv to cause mass casualties, the UAE’s top prosecutor said Friday.

In a statement carried by state-run news agency WAM, the official said the assailant carried out the attack “with the intention of causing the greatest possible number of human casualties.”

Authorities said Hammami was inspired by the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks in the U.S., and had taken two previous flights from Dubai to Tel Aviv to familiarize himself with the route and airport.

The findings shed new light on the Sept. 30 attack, which forced a FlyDubai passenger plane bound for Israel to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia after a violent struggle in the cockpit.

The axe-wielding assailant attacked Capt. Smit Machchhar, an Indian pilot with 17 years of flying experience, as the aircraft traveled over a region near Jordan and Saudi Arabia.

Despite suffering serious injuries, Machchhar managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew members to intervene as the plane rapidly lost altitude.

The aircraft plunged an estimated 14,000 to 16,000 feet in less than a minute before passengers were able to restrain the attacker and two reserve pilots took control. The plane safely landed in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.

After receiving treatment from hospitals in Saudi Arabia and Abu Dhabi, Machchhar later described the struggle during a video call with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

“When I was on the ground, I realized that the aircraft is going down,” Machchhar said in Hindi, according to a translation by The Associated Press. “And I told myself, ‘This is the last push, Smit. The door is right there.’”

Modi praised the captain for preventing what he described as another Sept. 11-style attack, saying he showed “the highest form of courage.”

In Friday’s statement, prosecutors said Hammami confessed to acting alone and provided a detailed account of his preparations and motives in the presence of his lawyer.
